item.content:encoded:
-As written, ice ghosts appear at exactly -37C and 125% humidity. No warmer and no colder. Seems more fitting that conditions need to be "…-37C or colder…" or perhaps "…where SCP-244-1 has changed the environmental temperature and humidity to conditions conducive to the persistence of ice fog…"
-Heatseekers are "far colder", but a real scientist would say precisely how much colder.
-Similarly, the actual temperature of the outside should be specified just like it is for the inside. It could be an interesting wrinkle if the outer surface matched the room like a normal vase, but still felt cold to people despite that.
-Containment would be better with a dedicated industrial strength dehumidifier to supplement temperature control.

There, nits have been picked.
+1

Now I indulge random imaginings…
This would make a great desperate measures security step, which I suppose is sort of what the CI was trying to do in the history section. Perimeter is breached, all intrusion countermeasures have failed, uncap the vase and evacuate! And bring the lid with you.

A version of The Foundation less wary of anomaly interactions would leave it open in the main warehouse and save on security overhead.
Or in the server room; free cryonics for all the superconducting processors you care to run.

item.content:encoded:
I enjoyed the concept, besides two little bits which bug me.

First, -37 degree vapor getting spit into a room is never going to actually reduce its temperature to -37 degrees. 1,000,000 parts of -37 degree air combined with one part of 10 degree air will average out to something a bit over the minimum threshold to set this thing off, as it's written.

Second, is this thing actually spitting out air or just converting the current air to a different temperature/humidity? The two imply very different effects. If it's actually spitting gas out, it'd be interesting to see what happens if you try to cover that up with something like a weather balloon.

Besides those, interesting SPC.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
The biggest draw this site has, and the main thing that sets us apart from simple creepypasta and fanfic, is that the SCP articles and related materials set a believable and realistic tone.

An SCP article is intended to read as a summary of containment procedures and the potential risks of failing to contain an SCP object written by a professional, clinical individual who knows what he's doing.

Lines like "we must have constant vigilance to be sure that the containment center does not become an icy waste." read like fanfic written by a high school student, not like a professional brief written by a serious scientist. They seriously breach character, and strongly damage suspention of disbelief. Frankly, it's a shitty thing to do to your article.

The entire final addendum adds precisely nothing to this article, and takes away quite a bit. You would be better off removing it.

"But someone else fucked up too!" is never a valid excuse.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Fair enough for the second part. I was going to try and mention ways the Foundation could crack open concrete if they needed to, but that would be either unnecessary detail or ridiculous inter-SCP reference wankery, neither of which would help this article.

As for the measurement to be used, first of all watts are already a rate measurement (joule per second) so saying kW/s is odd. Besides that though, this thing is really deterred by strong sources of thermal energy, right? We have a convenient measurement for that, and it's called temperature :D. Just give the thing a temperature, say 100 C, after which it avoids instead of pursues sources of heat.

As to yoric's comment and your reply, yes there are endnotes that lack the clinical tone of the normal SCP article. In my opinion the majority of them are unnecessary or even detrimental to the article. Even though they are notes tacked on to the official article, they are written by supposedly jaded professionals who deal with this sort of thing literally every day. It strains credibility (and reads awkwardly) for them to lapse into cheesy informal bickering at the end of every article despite the fact that they know it is going to be archived with the rest of the official document.

Some people have different opinions on that, which is doubtless why it is so popular. Heck I did it on first drafts of many of my articles. But I learned better, and at the very least expect to get this criticism every time you use that device in your writing here. With all that said, I don't think this article is a particularly notable offender but could benefit from some cleanup.

@Yoric: Why does an addendum need to be clinical? I've seen plenty on this site which seemed much more like personal notes than formal additions to a formal document.

@SimpleCadence: Don't worry about it; your science nitpicking teaches me a little more about physics, and I figure the lesson is worth the edit. Do you have any idea how many thermal watts burning wood might release? (100 kW/s is a wild guess).

Also, if you seal up the jar in concrete, you wouldn't be able to study it without cracking the concrete open. For the rest, I refer you to the second addendum and your imagination. Personally, I envision it somehow appearing outside of the container and tipping over. Or the container itself somehow splitting to accommodate the open jar. The scale-alarm system is more convenient than a lot of heavy-but-still-somehow-ineffective packaging and less expensive then trying to keep a fire burning inside a jar that constantly produces condensed water vapor.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
"This vapor is identical in composition to ice fog, with a temperature of zero (0) ℃ and 99% humidity as it exits SCP-244-1."

In an area of 99% humidity, all of the moisture in the air would be evaporated, thus invisible, thus you wouldn't get the creepy fog effect. Mist occurs once warmer air containing a lot of moisture cools down, passing the so-called "dew point" and condensing some of the air laden moisture into tiny droplets of fog. So any area with mist by definition has over 100% humidity (or has 100% humidity with further suspended liquid water, depending on how you define it).

Unless you are making this apparent contradiction a part of the artifact's strangeness, you should change the text to match. Also the measure "MJ/kg" isn't really a rate in the traditional sense, and depending on the amount of time involved the human body can indeed give off that ratio of thermal energy per kg of mass, so I think you wanted a power measurement there (Watts and the like).

As for containment, why can't they just wrap it up in something that allows no space for it to fall over and open? Like a form-fitted package? Or encase it in concrete? It seems unlikely that such a container would be overcome by the device as described, and if it does somehow have the ability to breach even that containment you might want to mention how it does so.

I'm sorry if I come off as overly critical, the science nitpicking usually brings out the most annoying of my editing habits.
